props.title: Teeth
props.initialSlug: Virginity pledge meets vagina dentata horror

sections.content: Teeth (2007) revolutionized body horror by weaponizing female sexuality through the vagina dentata myth. Director Mitchell Lichtenstein crafts a pitch-black comedy that's equal parts feminist revenge fantasy and coming-of-age nightmare. Like Ginger Snaps (2000) and Carrie (1976), it uses horror to explore female sexual awakening, but adds a savage critique of patriarchal control and sexual violence. The film's genius lies in making its protagonist Dawn both victim and monster, similar to the transformation in Raw (2016).

movies.title: Jennifer's Body
movies.slug: A possessed cheerleader preys on high school boys in this feminist horror-comedy written by Diablo Cody

sections.content: The film sits perfectly within the mid-2000s wave of extreme body horror that included Hostel (2005) and The Human Centipede (2009), but subverts their male-gazey exploitation by putting female revenge at the forefront. Dawn's journey from abstinence-pledging teen to avenging angel creates a fascinating character study that echoes Hard Candy (2005) in its exploration of gender power dynamics and retributive justice.

Like other feminist horror landmarks such as The Witch (2015) and A Girl Walks Home Alone at Night (2014), Teeth transforms perceived female weakness into strength. The film's dark humor helps balance its more extreme moments, making its commentary on sexual politics more digestible while never dulling its razor-sharp edge. movies.title: The Final Girls
movies.slug: A meta-horror comedy that sees modern teens trapped inside an 80s slasher film, subverting classic genre tropes

sections.content: Teeth paved the way for a new wave of horror films exploring female sexuality and bodily autonomy, including Fresh (2022) and Promising Young Woman (2020). Its influence can be seen in how these later films blend genres and use dark comedy to examine serious themes of consent, power, and revenge. The film's legacy continues in works like Titane (2021), which similarly uses body horror to challenge gender norms and sexual identity.
